def: Keshav's way of reading a paper in up to three passes (scan, grasp, re-create), stopping as soon as your question is answered.
The one sentence a paper's authors would defend, ideally with a headline number, a baseline and a stated condition.
An experiment that removes one component of a method to see how much the result depends on it.
The simpler or previous method a new result is compared against, which is only fair if it gets equal tuning, data and compute.
The smallest gap between two scores that sampling noise from the test-set size alone cannot explain.
Rerunning the authors' own code and data to see whether you obtain their reported numbers.
Testing the same finding with new data or a fresh implementation, which checks the finding rather than the reporting.
Keshav's first-pass questions: category, context, correctness, contributions and clarity.
A lab's description of a model or system, usually with less detail about what was tried and discarded than a research paper.
A structured reading of a field, built by following citations backwards and forwards from a few recent papers.
